meta.title: Tagalog A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 more words, none of them in A1 · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Tagalog → English (see the Tagalog, recall the meaning) and English → Tagalog (see an English meaning, recall the Tagalog). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be — Tagalog has no CEFR examination, and no openly licensed graded word list was found to build it from. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 465 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives, jobs, clothes, the kitchen and cooking, fruit, the rooms and things of a home, the town and its services, travel and transport, the natural world, animals, health and the body, feelings and character, free time and celebrations, school, the higher numbers and quantities, words for when and how often, more colours, describing things, the everyday verbs of doing, and the connectors and adverbs that join two sentences — and the other 285 are the commonest remaining words, by a frequency that averages two sources: a word list built from film and television subtitles, and the Tagalog sentences of Tatoeba, each counted per million words. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is spelt as ordinary Tagalog writing spells it, and beneath it Wiktionary's pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (735 of the 750) and, where the word carries one, its marked spelling, because ordinary writing shows neither the stress nor the final glottal stop (bata, a child, is batà). Verbs are given as the affixed verb you say (kumain, to eat), and the 140 verbs show their three aspects — completed, ongoing and contemplated (kumain, kumakain, kakain) — since Tagalog marks whether an action is done rather than when; where Wiktionary names it, a word shows its root and affix (kain + -um-). Real example sentences come with 717 of the 750 words, three apiece for 649 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, spellings, aspects and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0) and the Tatoeba corpus. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
